meta.title: Finance
meta.range: HSC topic · 25% of course time · interpreting financial information in planning and managing a business

boxes.label: Examinable
boxes.bodyHtml: Role of financial management, influences (internal/external sources of finance, financial institutions, government, global markets), processes (planning, debt/equity financing, monitoring via financial statements, financial ratios, limitations of financial reports, ethics) and financial management strategies (cash flow, working capital, profitability, global financial management) — all Learn To and Learn About dot points. Financial ratio formulas are provided in the real exam; COGS, gross profit, net profit and the accounting equation are not.

boxes.label: Format reminder
boxes.bodyHtml: The HSC Business Studies exam draws on all four topics: Section I is 20 multiple-choice questions, Section II is short-answer questions spanning all topics, Section III is a business-report extended response, and Section IV offers a choice of extended-response questions by topic.

summary.note: Organised by the syllabus's own headings for this topic.

groups.title: Role of financial management
points: The strategic role of financial management includes setting financial objectives, sourcing finance, preparing budgets and financial statements, maintaining sufficient cash flow, and distributing funds to other business functions.

The five objectives of financial management (SSPPMD): profitability (maximising profit — long and short term), growth (increasing size — long term), efficiency (minimising costs relative to assets — long term), liquidity (converting assets to cash to pay short-term debts — short term) and solvency (meeting all financial obligations, short and long term). Real example: Wesfarmers' FY2025 results show all five objectives being pursued together — group revenue of $45.7 billion (up 3.4%, growth), net profit after tax of $2,926 million (up 14.4%, profitability), and a return on equity of 34.3% (efficiency) — while its FY2025 dividend of 206 cents per share plus a proposed 150-cent capital return shows a business balancing reinvestment against returning cash to owners.

Interdependence: finance funds operations' investment in quality inputs and technology, funds HR's training and payroll, and funds marketing's advertising and promotion — while marketing's pricing and sales in turn generate the revenue finance manages.

groups.title: Influences on financial management
points: Internal finance is retained profits (profit after tax not distributed to shareholders).

External debt finance: short-term (overdraft, commercial bills, factoring) and long-term (mortgage, debentures, unsecured notes, leasing) — debt must eventually be repaid with interest, but doesn't dilute ownership.

External equity finance: ordinary shares (new issues/IPOs, rights issues, placements, share purchase plans) and private equity — funds don't need to be repaid, but ownership and control are diluted and profits are shared with new shareholders. Real example: after a collapse in revenue and regulatory findings against it, Star Entertainment survived only through a $300 million rescue package led by US operator Bally's and investor Bruce Mathieson — equity finance taken on the rescuer's terms after available cash fell to just $98 million against a $302 million half-year loss.

Key financial institutions: banks (loans, deposits, financial intermediation), investment banks (business-focused lending, mergers/underwriting advice), finance companies (smaller commercial loans, often at higher interest), superannuation funds (compulsory employer contributions), unit trusts (pooling many small investors' funds) and the Australian Securities Exchange (ASX) (Australia's primary and secondary share market).

ASIC (Australian Securities and Investments Commission) enforces the Corporations Act 2001 to protect consumers and investors from fraud; company taxation reduces a business's expected returns and must be accurately reported. Company tax is 30% (25% for base rate entities), and the imputation system is why Australian dividends are quoted as 'fully franked'.

Global market influences: a positive economic outlook increases demand for funding and access to borrowing; availability of overseas funds carries transaction exposure risk (exchange rate movements after a contract is signed); interest rates differ between countries, so businesses may borrow globally to access lower rates. The RBA cash rate — held at 4.35% at the August 2026 meeting — sets the domestic cost of debt finance; higher rates raise interest expense and make debt-funded expansion harder to sustain.

groups.title: Processes of financial management
points: Planning and implementing involves determining financial needs, developing budgets (operating, project and financial budgets), maintaining accurate record systems (e.g. the double-entry system), identifying financial risks, and establishing financial controls (like separating and rotating duties).

Debt financing advantages: funds available quickly, doesn't dilute ownership, interest is tax-deductible. Disadvantages: must pay interest, usually secured against an asset, increases financial risk. Equity financing advantages: no repayment obligation, low financial risk. Disadvantages: dilutes ownership, dividends aren't tax-deductible, shareholders gain voting rights.
The term of finance should match the asset's life — current assets should use short-term finance, non-current assets should use long-term finance, or the business risks serious cash flow problems.

Financial statements for monitoring and controlling: the cash flow statement (cash receipts and payments across operating, financing and investing activities), the income statement (revenue, cost of goods sold, gross profit, expenses, net profit) and the balance sheet (assets, liabilities and owner's equity at a point in time — Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity).

Limitations of financial reports: normalised earnings can exclude non-recurring items; capitalising expenses (recording an expense as an asset) can overstate profit; valuing assets (especially intangibles) can be inaccurate; timing issues let a business shift when revenue/expenses are recorded; debt repayment details and lengthy notes to the financial statements are often not fully disclosed or read. Real example: Woolworths and Coles had underpaid salaried managers for years using annualised salary 'set-off' arrangements. When the Federal Court found the practice unlawful in September 2025, an uncertain contingency became a very large liability almost overnight — Woolworths' estimated total potential liability is around $1.3 billion pre-tax, Coles' around $300 million — showing that reported accounts can be technically correct and materially incomplete for years before a legal ruling forces the true position onto the balance sheet.

Ethical financial reporting matters because owners, shareholders and lenders rely on honest reports — enforced through internal/external auditing and mandatory record-keeping for at least 5 years. Real example: ASIC won its first civil penalty cases over 'greenwashing' — misleading claims about the sustainability of investment products — with Vanguard Investments Australia fined $12.9 million, Mercer Superannuation $11.3 million, and Active Super $10.5 million (all 2024), after each was found to have invested in industries its marketing said were excluded. This shows the numbers in a report can be accurate while the narrative around them is misleading — exactly the gap ethical reporting is meant to close.

groups.title: Financial ratios
points: Current ratio (current assets ÷ current liabilities) measures liquidity — around 2:1 is considered sound.

Debt to equity (gearing) ratio (total liabilities ÷ total equity) measures solvency — around 1:1.5 is healthy; the lower the ratio, the less reliant on debt. Real example: Qantas held net debt of $5.0 billion at 30 June 2025, inside its target range of $4.6–5.7 billion — carrying meaningfully more gearing risk than Wesfarmers for a similar net profit margin.

Gross profit ratio (gross profit ÷ sales) and net profit ratio (net profit ÷ sales, around 10% is sound) measure profitability, as does return on equity (net profit ÷ total equity, around 10% is a benchmark). Real example: Wesfarmers' FY2025 net profit ratio was $2,926m ÷ $45,700m ≈ 6.4% — a supermarket-thin margin — yet its return on equity was 34.3%, showing the return was generated by high asset turnover and low equity rather than fat margins. Qantas' FY2025 net profit ratio was $1,605m ÷ $23,823m ≈ 6.7% — almost identical to Wesfarmers' — but earned while carrying $5.0 billion of net debt, the same margin with far more financial risk attached.

Expense ratio (total expenses ÷ sales) and accounts receivable turnover ratio (sales ÷ accounts receivable, then 365 ÷ that result for average collection days, ~30 days is efficient) measure efficiency. Real example: Mosaic Brands (Noni B, Millers, Rockmans and others) held inventory for around 128 days on average while paying its own suppliers on 120+ day terms — a working capital gap that eventually caught up with it, and the business entered voluntary administration in October 2024 owing creditors around $240–250 million.

Comparative ratio analysis gives a ratio context by comparing it over different time periods, against industry standards, or against similar businesses — but no two businesses are identical, so comparisons should be used as a guide, not an absolute judgement. Always name the ratio's family (liquidity, solvency, profitability, efficiency, growth) before naming the specific ratio, and always compare a figure to something — an unbenchmarked number is description, not analysis.

groups.title: Financial management strategies
points: Cash flow management strategies: distributing payments evenly across the year, offering discounts for early payment (improves cash flow but reduces profit margin), and factoring (selling accounts receivable for immediate cash, at a discount).

Working capital management controls current assets (cash, receivables, inventories) and current liabilities (payables, loans, overdrafts) — strategies include leasing and sale-and-lease-back to avoid large upfront asset purchases; to improve gearing, a business can decrease debt (sell non-essential assets, lease instead of buy) or increase equity (retain more profit, issue more shares). Real example: Star Entertainment's collapse to just $98 million in available cash against a $302 million half-year loss shows a business can fail on liquidity even while assets exist on paper — it is the textbook illustration that liquidity, not profitability alone, determines short-term survival.

Profitability management uses cost controls (managing fixed and variable costs, using cost centres, minimising expenses) and revenue controls (marketing objectives like pricing and sales mix) — efficiency can be improved by lowering the expense ratio or speeding up the accounts receivable turnover ratio. Real example: Mosaic Brands' operating profit margins stayed weak at 1–4.7% even at its peak (around $864 million revenue across roughly 1,400 stores) — evidence that growth through acquisition without cost control does not translate into profitability.

Global financial management: exchange rate appreciation/depreciation creates transactional and translational risk; businesses can exploit interest rate differentials by borrowing where rates are lower; international payment methods (payment in advance, letter of credit, clean payment, bill of exchange) balance risk between importer and exporter differently; hedging (using forward exchange contracts, options and swap contracts) reduces the risk of currency fluctuations.

questions.questionHtml: Explain a potential conflict between a business's short-term and long-term financial objectives.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Name two conflicting objectives.
  • Explain why achieving one can work against the other in the short run.
Sample answer

A possible conflict could occur between the long-term objective of efficiency and the short-term objective of profitability. Achieving efficiency in the long term could require an upfront investment in machinery, staff and technology, meaning money needs to be spent in the short term. This reduces short-term profitability, even though it reduces waste and leads to greater profit in the long term. A business focused only on short-term profit might avoid this investment, but would then miss out on the long-term efficiency gains and competitive advantage that come from it.

questions.questionHtml: Compare debt and equity as external sources of finance.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Define both.
  • Give at least one advantage and one disadvantage of each.
Sample answer

Debt finance (e.g. loans, debentures) must be repaid with interest, and is often secured against a business asset, which increases financial risk if the business defaults. However, it doesn't dilute ownership since lenders don't receive voting rights, repayments are predictable, and interest is tax-deductible, improving profitability.

Equity finance (e.g. issuing shares) doesn't need to be repaid and carries lower financial risk since there's no fixed repayment obligation — if the business fails, funds don't need to be returned to investors. However, it dilutes ownership and gives new shareholders voting rights, and dividends paid to shareholders aren't tax-deductible. A business's mix of debt and equity (its gearing) should reflect how much financial risk it's willing to take on relative to how much control it's willing to give up.

questions.questionHtml: Using a real example, explain how a decline in liquidity can force a business into dilutive equity finance.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain the difference between liquidity and profitability.
  • Support with a real, dated example.
  • Explain why equity was the only viable option.
Sample answer

Liquidity is a business's ability to convert assets to cash to meet short-term obligations, and is distinct from profitability — a business can be profitable on paper while still running out of cash to pay its bills. Star Entertainment demonstrates the difference clearly: it reported a statutory loss of $302 million for the half year to December 2024, with group revenue down 25%, and available cash of just $98 million.

With so little liquid cash and lenders only willing to extend waivers to 30 June, Star had no realistic option to raise debt finance, since a lender would be taking on a highly distressed borrower. It survived through a $300 million rescue package led by US operator Bally's and investor Bruce Mathieson — equity finance that diluted existing shareholders (whose shares were trading around 11 cents) but carried no repayment obligation, which was the only kind of finance a business in Star's liquidity position could realistically secure.

questions.questionHtml: A listed mining equipment manufacturer has cut its product-development spending by 45% and postponed a planned warehouse automation project, so it can hold its dividend steady with last year's payout. What tension between financial objectives does this decision reveal? Use the stimulus to support your answer.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Identify the two objectives in tension (growth/efficiency vs a stable return to shareholders).
  • Explain why prioritising one comes at the expense of the other.
  • Note the short-term vs long-term dimension.
Sample answer

This decision creates a conflict between the growth and efficiency objective and the objective of providing a stable return to shareholders. Cutting R&D and delaying automation preserves cash in the short term, letting the business maintain its dividend and keep shareholders satisfied now. However, R&D and automation investment are typically what drive a business's longer-term efficiency and competitiveness — by deferring them, the business risks falling behind competitors on cost or product development, which could threaten both future growth and its ability to sustain the same dividend in future years. The board has effectively chosen a stable short-term return over the business's longer-term growth and efficiency, and whether that trade-off was justified will depend on how essential the deferred project actually was to the business's competitive position.

questions.questionHtml: A logistics business has total liabilities of $58 million and total equity of $22 million. 70% of its debt is at variable interest rates. The cash rate has risen by 1 percentage point over the past year. Drawing on the stimulus, outline how this interest-rate movement is likely to affect the business.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Identify the business's high gearing (debt relative to equity).
  • Explain how a rate rise affects variable-rate debt specifically.
  • Link this to profitability and financial risk.
Sample answer

This business is already highly geared, with liabilities of $58 million against equity of only $22 million — a debt to equity ratio of roughly 2.6:1, well above what would usually be considered a conservative capital structure. Because 70% of that debt sits on variable interest rates, a 1 percentage point rise in the cash rate flows almost immediately into higher interest expense on the majority of its borrowings, without the business having agreed to that cost in advance the way it would have with fixed-rate debt.

This directly reduces net profit, since interest expense is deducted before net profit is calculated, and it increases the business's financial risk: a highly geared business with rising interest costs has less capacity to absorb a further rate rise or a downturn in revenue, since a larger share of its earnings before interest must go towards servicing debt rather than being available to owners or reinvested in the business.

questions.questionHtml: A business has current assets of $220,000 and current liabilities of $100,000. Calculate the current ratio, interpret what it means, and compare it to the industry benchmark of 2:1.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Apply the formula (current assets ÷ current liabilities).
  • Interpret the result in plain terms.
  • Compare to the 2:1 benchmark and make a judgement.
Sample answer

Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities = $220,000 ÷ $100,000 = 2.2:1. This means that for every $1 of current liabilities, the business has $2.20 in current assets available to cover it. This is slightly above the generally accepted industry benchmark of 2:1, indicating the business is in a sound liquidity position and should be able to meet its short-term obligations as they fall due. However, since the ratio is a little higher than the benchmark, the business could consider whether some of this cash might be better invested in non-current assets that would generate additional revenue over time, rather than sitting idle as current assets.

questions.questionHtml: Wesfarmers reported FY2025 net profit after tax of $2,926 million on revenue of $45,700 million. Qantas reported FY2025 statutory profit after tax of $1,605 million on revenue of $23,823 million. Calculate the net profit ratio for each business and compare them using comparative ratio analysis.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Apply the net profit ratio formula to both businesses and show the working.
  • Compare the two results.
  • Explain why the same ratio can still hide a large difference in risk.
Sample answer

Net profit ratio = net profit ÷ sales. Wesfarmers: $2,926m ÷ $45,700m ≈ 6.4%. Qantas: $1,605m ÷ $23,823m ≈ 6.7%. The two businesses achieved almost identical net profit ratios in FY2025, both a little below the general 10% benchmark for the ratio, reflecting the thin margins typical of retail and aviation.

However, comparative ratio analysis shouldn't stop at a single ratio in isolation. Qantas achieved its 6.7% margin while carrying net debt of $5.0 billion (within its target range of $4.6–5.7 billion), meaning a larger share of its business is funded by debt that must be repaid with interest regardless of performance. Wesfarmers, by contrast, achieved a similar margin with a return on equity of 34.3%, indicating its profit is generated efficiently from a comparatively smaller equity base without the same reliance on debt. Comparing net profit ratio alone would suggest the two businesses are equally profitable and equally exposed to risk — comparing gearing alongside it shows Qantas is earning the same margin while carrying substantially more financial risk.

questions.questionHtml: Explain why comparative ratio analysis is more useful than looking at a single financial ratio in isolation.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain the three bases of comparison (time, standards, similar businesses).
  • Note the limitation of comparing to other businesses.
Sample answer

A single financial ratio on its own has little meaning — comparative ratio analysis gives it context. Comparing a ratio over different time periods reveals whether a business's position is improving or declining. Comparing against industry standards shows how a business is performing relative to the broader market, though these standards are general and don't capture each business's individual circumstances. Comparing against similar, specific competitors can highlight where a business is excelling or falling behind. However, no two businesses are identical, so comparisons with competitors should be used carefully and as a guide rather than an absolute judgement of performance.

questions.questionHtml: Using the real example of Mosaic Brands, recommend how a business could use financial ratios to detect a working capital problem before it becomes insolvency.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Identify the relevant efficiency ratios.
  • Apply the real Mosaic Brands figures.
  • Recommend a specific monitoring strategy.
Sample answer

Efficiency ratios like inventory turnover and the accounts receivable/payable cycle can reveal a widening working capital gap well before a business becomes insolvent. Mosaic Brands (owner of Noni B, Millers, Rockmans and other fashion chains) held inventory for around 128 days on average while paying its own suppliers on terms of 120+ days — meaning the business was effectively financing its stockholding using supplier credit rather than its own cash, at operating margins that stayed weak (1–4.7%) even at peak revenue of around $864 million.

I would recommend the business track its inventory days and supplier payment days together every reporting period, rather than in isolation, since it's the gap between the two — not either figure alone — that signals the problem. Once inventory days consistently exceed supplier payment terms, as they did for Mosaic Brands, the business is relying on suppliers to fund growth. Mosaic Brands entered voluntary administration in October 2024 owing creditors an estimated $240–250 million, showing that stretching supplier terms is not a sustainable substitute for genuine working capital management — it only funds growth until suppliers stop extending credit.

questions.questionHtml: Pinnacle Physio — current assets $360,000; current liabilities $240,000. (a) Calculate the current ratio. (b) State what this figure suggests about the business's short-term financial position.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Apply the formula: current assets ÷ current liabilities.
  • State the result with its unit (a ratio, not a percentage).
  • Interpret the result against the 2:1 benchmark.
Sample answer

Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities = $360,000 ÷ $240,000 = 1.5:1 — Pinnacle Physio has $1.50 in current assets for every $1 of current liabilities due in the short term. This is below the generally accepted 2:1 benchmark, which suggests the business's short-term liquidity position is not especially strong — it may find it harder than a business at or above 2:1 to comfortably meet its short-term obligations if they all fell due at once, particularly if a portion of its current assets is inventory that cannot be quickly converted to cash. It doesn't necessarily mean the business is in financial trouble, but it is a ratio worth monitoring over time and comparing against the industry standard for a business of this type.

questions.questionHtml: Pinnacle Physio — sales $1,800,000; gross profit $810,000; net profit $216,000; total equity $600,000. (a) Calculate the gross profit ratio and the net profit ratio. (b) If the net profit ratio fell while the gross profit ratio stayed the same, what would this suggest?
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Calculate both ratios and state them as percentages.
  • Explain what an unchanged gross profit ratio alongside a falling net profit ratio means.
  • Suggest what the business should investigate.
Sample answer

Gross profit ratio = gross profit ÷ sales = $810,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 45%. Net profit ratio = net profit ÷ sales = $216,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 12%. If the gross profit ratio stayed unchanged while the net profit ratio fell, this tells us the problem is not with the cost of the services Pinnacle Physio sells relative to its sales revenue — that relationship is stable — but with its operating expenses, which have risen as a proportion of sales. Since gross profit less operating expenses equals net profit, a falling net profit ratio with a steady gross profit ratio points specifically to expenses such as wages, rent or marketing growing faster than revenue, and the business should investigate which specific expense category is driving the increase rather than assuming the problem lies in its core service pricing.

questions.questionHtml: Bayview Outfitters — year ended 30 June: sales $1,800,000, cost of goods sold $990,000, total expenses $594,000, net profit $216,000, current assets $300,000, current liabilities $150,000, accounts receivable $120,000, total liabilities $600,000, total equity $450,000. Work out five ratios from these figures — current, gross profit, debt to equity, expense, and accounts receivable turnover (in times and roughly how many days) — showing each calculation.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities.
  • Gross profit ratio = gross profit ÷ sales.
  • Debt to equity = total liabilities ÷ total equity.
  • Expense ratio = total expenses ÷ sales.
  • Accounts receivable turnover = sales ÷ accounts receivable, then 365 ÷ turnover for days.
Sample answer

Current ratio = $300,000 ÷ $150,000 = 2:1. Gross profit = sales − COGS = $1,800,000 − $990,000 = $810,000, so gross profit ratio = $810,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 45%. Debt to equity ratio = $600,000 ÷ $450,000 = 1.33:1. Expense ratio = $594,000 ÷ $1,800,000 = 33%. Accounts receivable turnover = $1,800,000 ÷ $120,000 = 15 times per year, which is approximately 365 ÷ 15 ≈ 24.3 days for Bayview Outfitters to collect its debts on average. As a check: sales $1,800,000 − COGS $990,000 − expenses $594,000 = $216,000, which matches the net profit given, confirming the figures are internally consistent.

questions.questionHtml: Recommend two strategies a business could use to improve its cash flow position.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Recommend two distinct strategies.
  • Explain how each improves cash flow, and note any trade-off.
Sample answer

A business could offer discounts for early payment, encouraging debtors who owe the largest amounts to pay sooner. This improves cash flow by bringing forward cash receipts, though it reduces the business's profit margin on those sales, and doesn't guarantee early payment will actually occur.

A business could also use factoring — selling its accounts receivable to a factoring company for a discounted price in exchange for immediate cash. This provides a fast cash injection and saves the business the cost and effort of chasing overdue payments itself, though it reduces the profit margin on those invoices and can damage customer relationships if the factoring company uses aggressive collection methods. Both strategies improve short-term liquidity at some cost to profitability, so a business should weigh which trade-off suits its current cash flow needs.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how hedging can help a business manage the risks of global financial transactions.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain the underlying risk hedging addresses (exchange rate fluctuation).
  • Describe at least one hedging method.
Sample answer

Businesses trading internationally face the risk that exchange rates will move unfavourably between signing a contract and making or receiving payment — an appreciation or depreciation of the Australian dollar can significantly change the real cost or revenue of a transaction. Hedging minimises this risk by reducing uncertainty around future currency movements.

One method is a forward exchange contract, where a business agrees to exchange currencies at a fixed rate on a set future date, regardless of how the market rate actually moves — this provides certainty over the cost of a future transaction. Another method is a currency option, which gives the buyer the right (but not the obligation) to exchange currency at a set rate in future, letting the business benefit if the market moves in its favour while still being protected if it doesn't, in exchange for paying a premium. By locking in or protecting against exchange rate movements, hedging helps a business plan its costs and revenue with more certainty.

questions.questionHtml: Using a real example, discuss why ethical financial reporting matters to a business's stakeholders.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain why stakeholders rely on financial reports being accurate.
  • Use a real, dated case as evidence.
  • Explain the consequence for the business.
Sample answer

Owners, shareholders and lenders rely on financial reports to make decisions — about whether to invest, lend, or continue holding shares — so misleading reporting doesn't just distort one company's numbers, it undermines the trust the whole financial system depends on.

ASIC's 2024 greenwashing cases show a modern version of this problem: Vanguard Investments Australia was fined $12.9 million, Mercer Superannuation $11.3 million, and Active Super $10.5 million, after each made claims about excluding certain industries (such as fossil fuels or gambling) from ethical investment products that turned out not to be true. In each case, the reported financial figures were accurate — the funds existed and performed as stated — but the narrative investors relied on to choose an ethical product was false.

This matters because investors specifically chose these products based on the ethical claims, meaning the misrepresentation directly affected their decision-making, not just their perception of the company. It shows that ethical financial reporting isn't only about the accuracy of the numbers on a balance sheet — it's about every representation a business makes to the people relying on its reports, and ASIC's willingness to pursue and win these cases signals that regulators now treat sustainability claims as seriously as any other financial disclosure.

questions.questionHtml: Explain how leasing and sale and lease back can improve a business's working capital.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain leasing.
  • Explain sale and lease back.
  • Note the shared trade-off.
Sample answer

Leasing improves working capital by letting a business use an asset such as equipment or a vehicle without paying its full purchase price upfront — instead, the business pays smaller periodic lease payments, freeing up cash that would otherwise be tied up in a large capital purchase, and keeping more current assets available for day-to-day operations. Sale and lease back goes further: a business that already owns an asset sells it to a financier for an immediate cash injection, then leases the same asset back to continue using it — this directly converts an illiquid non-current asset into liquid cash without disrupting operations, since the business keeps using the asset exactly as before. Both strategies improve short-term liquidity, but the trade-off is an ongoing lease expense and, with sale and lease back, the loss of any future capital gain on an asset the business no longer owns.

questions.questionHtml: An Australian electronics retailer imports stock priced in Japanese yen. Over the past year the Australian dollar has fallen from ¥95 to ¥88 per AUD. Drawing on the stimulus, outline the effect this exchange-rate movement has on the retailer's costs.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Explain that a falling AUD means more AUD are needed to buy the same amount of foreign currency.
  • Link this to the cost of imported stock in AUD terms.
  • Note the flow-on effect to profit margins or prices.
Sample answer

The Australian dollar has depreciated against the Japanese yen, falling from ¥95 to ¥88 per AUD. This means the retailer now receives fewer yen for each Australian dollar it converts, so it needs more Australian dollars than before to pay for the same yen-priced order of stock. Its cost of goods sold in Australian-dollar terms rises purely because of this currency movement, with no change in the actual yen price the supplier charges.

Unless the retailer can pass this higher cost on to customers through higher prices, its gross profit margin will be squeezed on every unit it imports. This illustrates why a business that sources internationally is exposed to exchange rate risk as a normal part of its financial management, even when nothing about its supplier relationship or the underlying product has changed.

questions.questionHtml: Silverline Traders — comparative ratios: current ratio this year 1.6:1, last year 2.1:1, industry 1.9:1; net profit ratio this year 8%, last year 11%, industry 10%; debt to equity this year 1.2:1, last year 0.8:1, industry 0.9:1. Drawing on the comparative figures given, assess how Silverline Traders' financial performance has changed.
questions.planHtml:
What to include
  • Assess liquidity using the current ratio trend and industry comparison.
  • Assess profitability using the net profit ratio trend and industry comparison.
  • Assess gearing/risk using the debt to equity trend and industry comparison.
  • Reach an overall judgement.
Sample answer

Silverline Traders' financial performance has weakened across all three ratios over the past year, and now sits below industry benchmarks on every measure. Its current ratio has fallen from 2.1:1 to 1.6:1, below the industry's 1.9:1, indicating declining short-term liquidity and a reduced buffer to meet short-term obligations. Its net profit ratio has fallen from 11% to 8%, below the industry's 10%, showing profitability has weakened relative to both its own recent history and its competitors. Most concerning is its debt to equity ratio, which has risen from 0.8:1 to 1.2:1, now above the industry's 0.9:1 — the business has become significantly more reliant on debt at exactly the time its profitability is falling, which increases its financial risk since it must service more debt with less profit. Taken together, these three ratios paint a consistent and worrying picture: Silverline Traders' overall financial performance has deteriorated on liquidity, profitability and gearing simultaneously, and each ratio reinforces the others — rising debt increases interest costs that further pressure the falling net profit ratio, while falling profitability makes it harder to rebuild the liquidity buffer that has also weakened.

trivia.questionHtml: What are the five objectives of financial management (SSPPMD)?
trivia.answerHtml: Solvency, profitability, growth, efficiency and liquidity.

trivia.questionHtml: What is retained profit?
trivia.answerHtml: The part of a business's after-tax profit that isn't distributed to shareholders — an internal source of finance.

trivia.questionHtml: What is an overdraft?
trivia.answerHtml: A short-term debt facility letting a business overdraw its account up to an agreed limit, useful for temporary cash shortfalls.

trivia.questionHtml: What is a debenture?
trivia.answerHtml: A loan from investors at a fixed interest rate, usually secured against an asset — a long-term debt source.

trivia.questionHtml: What does ASIC stand for and what does it enforce?
trivia.answerHtml: Australian Securities and Investments Commission — it enforces the Corporations Act 2001.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the current ratio formula and what does it measure?
trivia.answerHtml: Current assets ÷ current liabilities — measures liquidity; around 2:1 is considered sound.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the debt to equity (gearing) ratio formula and what does it measure?
trivia.answerHtml: Total liabilities ÷ total equity — measures solvency/reliance on debt; around 1:1.5 is healthy.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the net profit ratio formula?
trivia.answerHtml: Net profit ÷ sales — a ratio around 10% is generally considered sound.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the accounts receivable turnover ratio formula?
trivia.answerHtml: Sales ÷ accounts receivable — measures how efficiently a business collects its debts.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the accounting equation?
trivia.answerHtml: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity.

trivia.questionHtml: What is capitalising expenses?
trivia.answerHtml: Recording an expense as an asset on the balance sheet rather than as an expense on the income statement, which can overstate profit.

trivia.questionHtml: What is factoring?
trivia.answerHtml: Selling accounts receivable to a finance company at a discount, for immediate cash.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the difference between a cash flow statement and an income statement?
trivia.answerHtml: A cash flow statement records cash receipts/payments over time; an income statement summarises income earned and expenses incurred to calculate profit.

trivia.questionHtml: What is working capital?
trivia.answerHtml: The funds available for a business's short-term financial commitments — current assets minus current liabilities.

trivia.questionHtml: What is sale and lease back?
trivia.answerHtml: Selling an owned non-current asset to a lessor, then leasing it back through fixed payments.

trivia.questionHtml: What is transactional risk?
trivia.answerHtml: The risk of increased cost from an adverse change in exchange rates when making an international transaction.

trivia.questionHtml: What is hedging?
trivia.answerHtml: Strategies used to minimise the risk of currency fluctuations in international financial transactions.

trivia.questionHtml: What is a forward exchange contract?
trivia.answerHtml: A contract to exchange currencies at an agreed rate on a future date, reducing exchange rate risk.

trivia.questionHtml: What is normalised earnings?
trivia.answerHtml: Earnings adjusted to exclude non-recurring items, to give a more accurate picture of ongoing business performance.

trivia.questionHtml: Name one unethical financial reporting practice and a real company linked to it.
trivia.answerHtml: Misrepresenting financial statements — Enron overstated revenue and understated spending.

trivia.questionHtml: How long must Australian businesses keep financial records?
trivia.answerHtml: At least 5 years.

trivia.questionHtml: What is the difference between a fixed and a variable cost?
trivia.answerHtml: Fixed costs don't change with production/sales levels (e.g. rent); variable costs change directly with them (e.g. wages tied to output).

trivia.questionHtml: What was Wesfarmers' FY2025 net profit ratio, and what did its 34.3% return on equity reveal about it?
trivia.answerHtml: Around 6.4% net profit ratio — a thin margin, but a high ROE showed the return came from asset turnover and low equity, not fat margins.

trivia.questionHtml: What was Qantas' net debt at 30 June 2025, and what was its target range?
trivia.answerHtml: $5.0 billion, inside its target range of $4.6–5.7 billion.

trivia.questionHtml: What caused Star Entertainment's liquidity crisis reported in its half-year results to December 2024?
trivia.answerHtml: A statutory loss of $302 million, revenue down 25%, and available cash of just $98 million.

trivia.questionHtml: How did Star Entertainment survive its 2024–25 liquidity crisis?
trivia.answerHtml: A $300 million equity rescue package led by Bally's and investor Bruce Mathieson.

trivia.questionHtml: What working capital problem led to Mosaic Brands' voluntary administration in October 2024?
trivia.answerHtml: It held inventory for around 128 days while paying suppliers on 120+ day terms — a widening gap it couldn't sustain, leaving it owing $240–250 million.

trivia.questionHtml: What was Mosaic Brands' peak revenue, and how weak were its operating margins even then?
trivia.answerHtml: About $864 million across ~1,400 stores, with operating margins of only 1–4.7%.

trivia.questionHtml: What is 'greenwashing', and which three Australian financial firms were penalised for it by ASIC in 2024?
trivia.answerHtml: Misleading claims about a product's sustainability — Vanguard ($12.9m), Mercer ($11.3m) and Active Super ($10.5m).

trivia.questionHtml: What did the Federal Court find about Woolworths and Coles in September 2025?
trivia.answerHtml: That both had unlawfully underpaid salaried managers using annualised salary 'set-off' arrangements, affecting close to 30,000 employees.

trivia.questionHtml: What is Woolworths' estimated total potential liability from the underpayment ruling?
trivia.answerHtml: Around $1.3 billion pre-tax, once interest, superannuation and payroll tax are included.

trivia.questionHtml: What was the RBA cash rate held at, at the August 2026 meeting?
What Australian company tax rate applies to most large businesses?
trivia.answerHtml: 30% (25% for base rate entities).
